To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the minimal ablative margins (MAM) after stereotactically guided radiofrequency ablation of hepatocellular carcinomata are an independent predictor of tumor progression, with MAM > 5 mm correlating to no local tumor progression (p < 0.05) and that image fusion is a feasible and useful tool to determine MAM intraoperatively.

the minimal ablative margins (MAM) after stereotactically guided radiofrequency ablation is the only significant predictor of local tumor progression (p = 0,036), that a MAM of more than 5 mm is necessary to consider the ablation successful, and that image fusion using commercially available registration software is possible.
the minimal ablative margins are the only significant independent predictors for local tumor progression (OR =0.7, p =0.036).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to improve the treatment of patients with HCC by means of RFA.
the development of an image fusion algorithm for the intraoperative determination of the minimal ablational margin (MAM).
the question of how the MAM can be determined and how this can be used as a predictor of local tumor progression (p = 0,036) in patients treated with a stereotactic RFT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

MAM is a significant and independent predictor of local tumor progression in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma treated with SRFA, but that the results are not conclusive enough to use MAM as a reliable predictor of treatment success.
a MAM >5 mm correlates well with complete remission, and a MAM ≤5 mm correlates significantly with local tumor progression.
the MAM is a reliable tool to evaluate the success of a SRFA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MAM is an independent predictor of local tumor progression after SRFA of HCC and a MAM >5 mm can be used as a successful treatment outcome.
a minimal ablative margin of 5 mm is the only independent predictor for local progression-free survival.
a MAM >5 mm has a high probability to achieve complete remission and therefore a high probability of no local tumor progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a minimal ablative margin of > 5 millimeters is required to achieve complete remission after SRFA.
an intraoperatively measured MAM >  5 mm correlates with complete remissions and can be used as a tool to determine treatment success.
an immediate assessment of the MAM can be used as a tool to evaluate the outcome of SRFA.
